full_instruction: Write a short, deliberately cheesy romance story about a late-night radio host who receives anonymous song requests from the same caller every evening. The host slowly realises the caller is someone they know. Write the story through dialogue and brief narration. Include a song dedication that becomes an accidental confession. Include the exact sentence, “You have been broadcasting into my heart for months.” End with the caller appearing outside the studio window.

constraints.requirement: A late-night radio host as a main character
An anonymous caller who calls every evening as a main character
The caller requests a song every evening
The host slowly realises the caller is someone they already know
Write the story through dialogue and brief narration
Include a song dedication that becomes an accidental confession
Include the exact sentence, "You have been broadcasting into my heart for months."
End with the caller appearing outside the studio window

text:
"It's 2:14 AM!" Mike boomed into the microphone, his smile blinding even in the dark studio. "This is *Midnight with Mike*, Tri-State County's premier destination for love, mystery, and terrible puns! And tonight... we have a caller who has been haunting my frequency for three months straight!"

He leaned closer to the phone, his voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper. "Who is he? Is he an alien? A ghost? Or perhaps... *The Velvet Voice*?"

On the other end, a smooth, baritone crackled through the static. "Hi, Mike. How are you?"

"I'm fantastic! You sound like an angel singing in a library made of velvet!" Mike declared, throwing his hands up as if conducting an invisible orchestra. The studio engineer nodded along enthusiastically. "Gary, darling! You're on the air! Tell me, what is your real name? Do you have a secret girlfriend? Are you actually a spy from the Cold War?"

"I'm telling you," Gary said, his voice dropping to a sultry whisper that made the whole room turn a shade of red, "my real name is irrelevant. What matters is that tonight, at 2:15 AM, I am falling in love with your laugh."

The entire studio went silent except for the hum of the air conditioning. Mike's eyes widened comically. He looked at Sarah, his producer, who was trying desperately not to smile while sipping her lukewarm coffee.

"Gary!" Mike gasped, clutching his chest as if he'd been shot. "You have me! You've won my heart! But tell me, darling, if we were together, what would our first dance be?"

"It would be the waltz," Gary said softly. "But I'd only ask you to dance if you promised to never let go."

"I promise!" Mike screamed into the mic, doing a little spin in his chair that nearly knocked over his water glass. "I'd hold on so tight my knuckles would turn white! We'll dance until the sun comes up and we're both too tired to walk!"

"Mike," Gary said, his voice trembling with emotion, "you're making this awkward."

"Awkward?" Mike laughed, wiping a tear from his eye. "Gary, darling, you are making me romantic! You are turning my studio into a fairy tale! But before we get too deep, I need to ask about your nightly ritual."

Gary cleared his throat. The smooth jazz track in the background paused abruptly.

"Every evening," Gary recited with perfect cadence, "I request that you play 'Unchained Melody' right after my call ends. And if you skip it, I will haunt your voicemail for eternity."

Mike gasped dramatically, clutching his heart. "Oh, Gary! You are so sweet! So demanding! So *perfect*!" He turned to the crowd, shouting, "Ladies and gentlemen, does this man know he's already my soulmate? Because 'Unchained Melody' is now our sacred vow!"

Sarah raised her eyebrows. "Mike, that's not a request; that's an order."

"It's a love song, Sarah! It's music from the heart!" Mike insisted, beaming. "Tell me, Gary, if we were to record this special edition of the show, what would our title be?"

"'Gary's Eternal Request: The Unchained Edition,'" Gary supplied instantly.

"And I'll adore you back a million times over!" Mike shouted, throwing his arms up triumphantly as the backup lights flashed rhythmically. "This is the best night ever! We are officially *it*!"

Sarah finally cracked a smile and picked up her pen to write down the show's new tagline: *"Love in the Static, with Unchained Melody."*

As the clock struck 2:15 AM, Mike leaned back into his mic, beaming. "And now, Gary, tell everyone why you called tonight!"

Gary paused, then said in a voice that sounded like honey poured over gravel, "Because I finally found the only voice on earth I want to listen to forever, and because I know exactly which song will make your heart skip a beat."

The crowd went wild, cheering and clapping, while Mike smiled so broadly he thought his face might split right down the middle. It was cheesy, it was ridiculous, and honestly? It was perfect.

"Alright!" Mike announced to the empty studio, "Let's play 'Unchained Melody' for Gary! And remember, folks, if you don't hear it tonight, just call me in your dreams!"

The speakers crackled with static, followed by the sweet, soaring vocals of Roy Orbison. Mike closed his eyes, swaying gently to the rhythm, completely lost in the moment—until he heard a familiar laugh echoing through his memory.

He stopped dancing. He dropped his pen. His eyes snapped open, wide and terrified.

"Wait," Mike whispered, staring at the phone line as if it were a cobra. "Gary... you requested 'Unchained Melody' every single night for three months."

"Yeah?" Gary's voice came through, smooth and confident.

"And you never mentioned your name," Mike said, his voice shaking. "You never mentioned where you live. You never mentioned that you work at the Diner on 5th Street."

"Oh, come on," Gary chuckled softly. "Don't tell me you forgot my lunch order?"

Mike froze. "The extra pickle? The ketchup packet shaped like a heart?"

"That's right." A pause. Then, a giggle that sounded suspiciously like Mike's own voice from three years ago. "And don't tell me you forgot that I'm the reason you stopped dating because you said you were too busy being 'romantic'."

Mike looked at Sarah. "Is it... is it possible?" he whispered to the empty room. "Is it possible that the 'Velvet Voice' isn't a stranger, but the guy who brought me donuts every Monday for a year while I tried to write my memoir?"

"Obviously," Gary replied, his voice dropping an octave into pure panic-mode whispering. "I'm Dave! Your ex-boyfriend! The one who dated you in college until you said 'I need space' because I was too good at listening!"

The studio lights flickered violently. Sarah dropped her pen and screamed, "MIKE! IT'S DAVE!"

Mike stared at the phone, his heart pounding a million miles an hour. "Dave," he squeaked into the microphone, "why are you calling me at 2:15 AM to tell me you're in love with my laugh?"

"Because," Dave said, his voice cracking slightly, "I missed you. And I still like your laugh. Even if you *did* break up with me because I was 'too nice'."

Mike slumped back into his chair, the neon glow of the studio suddenly feeling very small. "So," Mike stammered, "the mystery caller... is my ex?"

"Yes!" Dave confirmed triumphantly. "And I still want to hear 'Unchained Melody' every night! Even if you did cheat on me with a guy named Steve!"

"I did not cheat on you with Steve!" Mike yelled at the phone. "Steve was just a friend who listened to my music!"

"Whatever you say, Mike," Dave sighed, sounding less like a romantic lead and more like a confused roommate. "Just please play the song before I hang up. My shift ends in ten minutes."

Mike looked at the crowd, then at the mic. The romance was gone. The mystery was solved. But as he hit the button to play 'Unchained Melody,' he realized something strange: he actually wanted Dave on the radio. Maybe not as a boyfriend, but as a permanent fixture of his life.

"Alright!" Mike shouted, grinning uncontrollably despite himself. "Let's hear that song, Dave! And maybe... we can get coffee tomorrow?"

Dave laughed, and for the first time in years, Mike felt like he wasn't alone in the studio. It wasn't cheesy anymore; it was just real.

"And remember," Mike added as the music swelled, "if you skip this song, I'll haunt your voicemail!"

"Deal," Dave replied. "But only if you promise to stop writing memoirs about my 'terrible' cooking."

"Never," Mike vowed. "Your pot roast is legendary."

It was cheesy, it was ridiculous, and honestly? It was perfect.

Suddenly, the studio DJ cut the music abruptly. "Hey Mike!" the control room voice crackled in his earpiece. "We got a call from your sister! She says she heard you talking to 'The Velvet Voice' and wants to know if you're dating anyone new!"

Mike froze. The song 'Unchained Melody' was still playing softly in the background, but now it sounded like a funeral dirge.

"Mike!" Sarah hissed, leaning over the console. "Your mom is calling! She thinks you're proposing to a ghost because you haven't hung up on her yet!"

Mike grabbed the phone again. "Dave," he said urgently, "my family is about to invade this studio via satellite link. Do you have anything to say before they hear us?"

Dave paused. The static hissed loudly. Then, in a voice that was suddenly very steady and very clear, he said: "Mike? If your family asks... just tell them I'm the one who taught you how to change a tire when you were sixteen. And maybe... maybe you could let me pick up dinner on Thursday?"

There was a long silence. The only sound was the fading outro of Roy Orbison and the sudden, awkward cackle of Mike's own mother laughing in her living room three states away.

"It's not a confession!" Mike yelled into the mic, his face turning bright red. "It's... it's a logistical proposal for a dinner date! Just like old times!"

Dave chuckled softly. "Right. Old times. Sounds great."

"Old times," Mike repeated, staring at the phone with dawning horror and realization. "Yeah. Definitely old times."

He looked at Sarah. "Sarah, turn off the mic. And call my mom back and tell her I'm... I'm still single!"

"I can't do that, Mike," Sarah said flatly. "The show is live. And the audience is already voting 'Soulmates' on the app."

Mike sighed, slumped into his chair, and smiled a small, genuine smile. "Well," he muttered to the phone, "at least the song dedication worked out better than I expected."

Dave laughed again. "Good. Because next week, I'm dedicating 'Sweet Caroline' to you. No matter what you say."

"And if you skip it," Mike warned playfully, "I'll haunt your voicemail!"

"Deal," Dave replied. "But only if you promise to stop writing memoirs about my 'terrible' cooking."

"Never," Mike vowed. "Your pot roast is legendary."

It was cheesy, it was ridiculous, and honestly? It was perfect.

"You have been broadcasting into my heart for months," Mike suddenly blurted out, forgetting every rule of radio etiquette in the world. He immediately covered his mouth with both hands. "I mean—wait! No! That's not what I meant! I meant you've been a great caller!"

Dave laughed softly, and this time, there was no static between them. "That," he said, "is the most cheesy thing I've ever heard. And honestly? I think it's true."

Then, Mike heard a soft knock at the glass partition separating the studio from the control booth. He looked up through the small window in the door. Standing outside wasn't a fan, not a producer, and certainly not a ghost. It was Dave, wearing his usual diner apron over a flannel shirt, holding two mugs of coffee, smiling with that same familiar warmth.

"Hey, Mike," Dave called out, his voice clear without the phone's filter. "I said I'd be here if you needed me. And since you missed my shift ending ten minutes ago, I figured I'd just swing by and say hi."

Mike stared at him, then slowly reached into his pocket and pulled out a slightly crumpled note that read: *'For the guy who makes the best pot roast.'*

"Well," Mike squeaked, standing up and grabbing his jacket, "since you're already here... maybe we can skip the radio bit and just get coffee?"

Dave grinned, walking around to the door handle. "Only if you promise to tell your mom I'm not a ghost."

"I'll do my best," Mike said, unlocking the door.

As they stepped out of the studio together into the cool night air, the crowd in the booth cheered one last time, realizing that the best romance story of all wasn't on the airwaves—it was happening right outside the window.
